The excerpt adds that if you have no other choice than updating in-use CIDRs, the node-group migration procedure should be used as a reference instead.

optionRationale.b: Replacing an in-use CIDR is an update to a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt says is not possible; the worked example only gets there by splitting the cluster into two node groups and migrating workloads.
optionRationale.c: Removing a CIDR is a deletion of a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt explicitly rules out.
optionRationale.d: Shrinking an in-use CIDR is still an update to a CIDR already in use, so it is not among the permitted changes.

In a Kubernetes Secret in the `kube-system` namespace, referenced by the Cilium agent DaemonSet.
In the `cilium-config` ConfigMap, under a per-node key entry.
In the status field of a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` object scoped to the node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names an annotation on a ``CiliumNode`` object, not a Secret.
optionRationale.c: No ConfigMap is mentioned as the distribution mechanism for node public keys.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator wants to mitigate the risk of unencrypted egress traffic to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints by ensuring that traffic exiting a node to a specific set of IP addresses is always encrypted. Which configuration should they apply?

options.text: Set encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and define the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr.
Enable encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to drop any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive via the WireGuard tunnel.
Configure a network policy that allows egress traffic to reserved:world identities to ensure all external traffic is routed through the tunnel.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false to block all traffic associated with node identities.

questions.explanation: The excerpt identifies setting encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr as a way to mitigate the issue by enforcing that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

optionRationale.b: Strict mode ingress protects local endpoints from unencrypted ingress traffic, not egress traffic from the node to remote endpoints.
optionRationale.c: Allowing traffic to reserved:world is identified as a condition that makes the unencrypted leak possible, not a mitigation. The mitigation is to restrict this or use strict mode.
optionRationale.d: Setting allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false is not the primary mitigation described for the general pod CIDR; it is a specific setting related to node identities when not using direct routing mode.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: Another way to mitigate this issue is to set ``encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled`` to ``true`` and the expected pod CIDR as ``encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr``. This encryption strict mode egress enforces that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

questions.stem: An engineer defines a Cilium Layer 7 HTTP policy rule that sets a Path regex but leaves the Method field empty. A client sends a POST request whose path matches the regex. What is the result?

options.text: The request is allowed, because an omitted or empty Method permits all methods.
The request is denied, because a Method must be specified explicitly for an HTTP rule to match.
The request is allowed only if it is a GET request, because GET is the default method.
The request is evaluated by matching the POST method against the Path regex.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if Method is omitted or empty, all methods are allowed. The POST request is therefore permitted when its path matches the Path regex, and no separate Method value is required.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not require Method to be set; an omitted or empty Method allows all methods rather than causing a denial.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says all methods are allowed when Method is omitted or empty, not that GET becomes the only permitted method.
optionRationale.d: Method is matched against the method of a request, while Path is matched against the path of a request; the two fields are not interchangeable.

citations.title: HTTP
citations.quote: Method is an extended POSIX regex matched against the method of a request, e.g. ``GET``, ``POST``, ``PUT``, ``PATCH``, ``DELETE``, ...  If omitted or empty, all methods are allowed.

questions.stem: After TLS has been enabled on the Hubble metrics API, a monitoring engineer finds that Prometheus can no longer scrape the metrics endpoint. What does the excerpt say must be done to the Prometheus scrape configuration?

options.text: Update the scrape configuration to use HTTPS by setting a tls_config and provide the path to the CA certificate.
Leave the scrape configuration on HTTP, because TLS applies only to the Hubble observer API.
Switch the scrape target to HTTPS; no tls_config or CA certificate path is needed.
Provide a client certificate and key, but keep scraping over plain HTTP.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that when TLS is used with the Hubble metrics API, the Prometheus scrape configuration must be updated to use HTTPS by setting a tls_config and providing the path to the CA certificate. A client certificate and key are an additional requirement only when mTLS is in use.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says the scrape configuration must be updated to use HTTPS, so leaving it on HTTP is wrong.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires both HTTPS and a tls_config carrying the path to the CA certificate.

questions.stem: A caller issues a `GetFlows` request that supplies both an allow list and a deny list. A particular flow matches the allow list and also matches the deny list. What does the caller receive?

options.text: The flow is absent from the result, because the result contains only flows matched by the allow list that are not simultaneously matched by the deny list.
The flow is present, because a flow only needs to match one of the supplied filters to be included.
The flow is present, because the allow list always takes precedence over the deny list when both are supplied.
The flow is present twice, once for the allow list match and once for the deny list match.

questions.explanation: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result contains all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list. A flow that matches both lists is therefore excluded. The rule that only one of multiple flow filters has to match applies to filters of the same kind, and it does not override the interaction between an allow list and a deny list.

optionRationale.b: The 'only one has to match' rule describes multiple flow filters of the same kind; it does not mean a flow matching both an allow and a deny list survives.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: flows matched by the allow list are removed when they are also simultaneously matched by the deny list.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes duplicate delivery; the deny list removes flows from the allow list result rather than adding to it.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result will contain all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

questions.stem: A Hubble instance has been running for a long time and its ring buffer has become full, while a ring reader in follow mode continues to read events as they are written. What happens to the events already stored in the buffer?

options.text: They are overridden by newer events, because events are continuously consumed and older ones are overridden once the ring buffer is full.
They are retained indefinitely and new events are dropped until the reader has drained the buffer.
They are written out to disk so that the in-memory buffer can be reused.
They are preserved because the ring buffer grows dynamically to accommodate new events.

questions.explanation: Hubble stores monitoring events in a user-space ring buffer that holds a configurable amount of events in memory. Events are continuously consumed, overriding older ones once the ring buffer is full, so the oldest stored events are lost as new ones arrive.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes older events being overridden, not new events being dropped while the reader catches up.
optionRationale.c: The buffer is described as storing events in memory; no spilling of events to disk is mentioned.
optionRationale.d: The buffer stores a configurable amount of events and overrides older ones when full; it is not described as growing dynamically.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: Events are continuously consumed, overriding older ones once the ring buffer is full.

questions.stem: You are validating a Hubble installation and run `kubectl get configmap -n kube-system cilium-config -oyaml | grep hubble-disable-tls`. The output shows `hubble-disable-tls: "false"`. What does this tell you before you proceed with the remaining validation steps?

options.text: TLS has been configured correctly for Hubble, because the option that would disable it is set to false.
TLS is currently disabled for Hubble and must be switched on before any further validation can take place.
The value is a placeholder written by the Hubble CLI pod, which has not yet been created in the cluster.
Hubble Relay is running, but the Hubble server certificate has expired and must be renewed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to verify the configuration before beginning, and states that you should see the `hubble-disable-tls` configuration option set to `false`. A value of `false` therefore means TLS is not being disabled, that is, it has been configured correctly, and you can continue with the validation procedure.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the meaning of the flag: `false` means TLS is not disabled, so it is not a signal that TLS must be switched on.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt presents the check as the first step, performed before the Hubble CLI pod is created, and attaches no placeholder meaning to the value.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing here about certificate expiry; expiry is not what this configuration option reports.

citations.title: Validating the Installation
citations.quote: You should see that the ``hubble-disable-tls`` configuration option is set to ``false``.

questions.stem: An engineer wants the Hubble metrics API to require clients to authenticate with certificates. She has already created a ConfigMap named hubble-metrics-ca in the kube-system namespace from a file called ca.crt. Which combination of Helm flags does the excerpt prescribe?

options.text: --set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true, --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true only
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=ca.crt
--set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs the reader to add three flags to the Helm command to enable mTLS: the base TLS flag, the mTLS flag, and the flag naming the ConfigMap that holds the CA certificate. All three are required together.

optionRationale.b: Enabling mTLS alone omits both the base TLS flag and the name of the ConfigMap holding the CA certificate.
optionRationale.c: The name flag takes the name of the ConfigMap (hubble-metrics-ca), not the name of the file used to create it.
optionRationale.d: This omits the flag that actually enables mTLS authentication, so client certificates would not be required.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 with Hubble metrics already enabled. They want the Hubble metrics API to be served over TLS, but they do not want Prometheus to have to present a client certificate. Which single Helm option should they add to their install or upgrade command?

options.text: --set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca
--set hubble.tls.enabled=true

optionRationale.b: This flag enables mTLS authentication on the metrics API, which would require clients to present certificates — more than the team asked for.
optionRationale.c: This flag only names the ConfigMap holding the CA certificate; it is used alongside the mTLS flags and does not on its own turn on TLS.

questions.stem: From the Hubble CLI pod you query the first peer with `hubble observe --server tls://${IP?}:4244 --tls-server-name ${SERVERNAME?} --tls-ca-cert-files /var/lib/hubble-relay/tls/hubble-server-ca.crt`, deliberately omitting the client certificate and key. What happens, and why?

options.text: The command fails with exit code 1 and a TLS error stating that a certificate is required, because the server expects clients to present a certificate.
The command succeeds, because supplying the CA certificate file is sufficient to authenticate the client to the server.
The command fails with `error reading server preface: EOF`, because the server only accepts plaintext connections on that port.
The command succeeds but returns only flows involving the host endpoint, since unauthenticated clients see a restricted view.

questions.explanation: The excerpt contrasts two attempts: one using the Hubble Relay client certificate, which confirms that the server accepts clients presenting the correct certificate, and one made without any client certificate, which fails with a TLS error reporting that a certificate is required and terminates with exit code 1. The CA file alone verifies the server; it does not authenticate the client.

optionRationale.b: The CA certificate file is used to verify the server's certificate; the excerpt shows the connection still failing when no client certificate is supplied.
optionRationale.c: The `EOF` error belongs to the separate attempt made without TLS at all, not to a TLS connection that lacks a client certificate.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the command terminating with exit code 1 rather than returning a restricted set of flows.

questions.stem: An engineer is reasoning about how many events a Hubble ring buffer can hold, having read that the internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1. Which statement describes the capacity from a user perspective?

options.text: The capacity is one less than a power of 2, because one slot is reserved for the writer.
The capacity is exactly a power of 2, with every slot available to readers.
The capacity is one more than a power of 2, because the writer slot is added on top of the mask.
The capacity is exactly the configured number of events, with no slot reserved for the writer.

questions.explanation: The internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1, and the internal buffer size is always a power of 2 with 1 slot reserved for the writer. From a user perspective this means the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

optionRationale.b: A power of 2 is the internal buffer size, but one slot is reserved for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is one less than that.
optionRationale.c: The reserved writer slot is taken out of the power-of-2 size rather than added to it, so the capacity is one less, not one more.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly reserves one slot for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is not the full configured figure.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: In effect, from a user perspective, the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

questions.stem: How does enabling mTLS on the Hubble metrics API change what clients such as Prometheus must do, compared with plain TLS on the same API?

options.text: Clients must authenticate using a certificate signed by the configured CA certificate.
Clients must supply a username and password alongside the HTTPS request.
Clients must present a bearer token issued by the Hubble observer API.
Clients are unaffected, because mTLS applies only to the Hubble observer API.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that after the mTLS configuration is applied, clients are required to authenticate using a certificate signed by the configured CA certificate in order to access the Hubble metrics API. Plain TLS does not impose that client-authentication step.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes certificate-based authentication, not a username and password.
optionRationale.c: No token mechanism is mentioned; authentication is by certificate signed by the configured CA.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt applies this requirement to the Hubble metrics API itself, so clients are affected.

citations.title: Hubble Metrics TLS and Authentication
citations.quote: clients will be required to authenticate using a certificate signed by the configured CA certificate to access the Hubble metrics API.

questions.stem: You have created the Hubble CLI pod in `kube-system` and run `hubble watch peers --server unix:///var/run/cilium/hubble.sock`. Peers are listed, but no `TLS.ServerName` appears beside them. What does this indicate?

options.text: TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server, and the following validation steps will not work.
TLS is enabled, but the server name is only shown for peers that are reached through Hubble Relay rather than the local socket.
The Hubble CLI pod is missing the relay client certificate, so the server name cannot be resolved.
The peers are healthy; the server name is only displayed when `--tls-server-name` is passed to `hubble watch peers`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt warns explicitly that if the `TLS.ServerName` is missing from the output, TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server and the following steps will not work, and it directs you back to the previous sections to enable TLS. The absence of the field is therefore a signal about the server's TLS configuration, not about the CLI pod's credentials.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt draws no distinction between peers reached over the socket and peers reached through the relay; the missing field simply means TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server.
optionRationale.c: The command is run against the local socket, and the excerpt attributes a missing server name to TLS not being enabled on the server, not to a missing client certificate.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no such flag for `hubble watch peers`; the server name appears in the peer listing itself when TLS is enabled.

questions.stem: An engineer configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. During a specific flow, the DNS name for the destination is not known. What value will be used for the `destination` label in the metric?

options.text: The IP address of the destination
An empty string
The Kubernetes namespace of the destination
The reserved identity label

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when multiple contexts are specified, the first non-empty value is added to the metric as a label. It explicitly gives the example that if no DNS name is known, it will fall back and use the IP address of the target instead.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that the first non-empty value is used, implying a fallback occurs rather than an empty label being forced if a subsequent option is available.
optionRationale.c: The namespace is not part of the specified `dns|ip` chain, so it is not considered for the fallback.
optionRationale.d: The reserved identity is not part of the specified `dns|ip` chain, so it is not considered for the fallback.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to narrow down Cilium datapath debug events by supplying allow and deny filters to the `GetDebugEvents` RPC endpoint, in the same way they do for `GetFlows`. What is the outcome?

questions.stem: In the context of Cilium Ingress, how many logical Policy enforcement points are identified in the excerpt, and what are the transitions between them?

options.text: One enforcement point, where traffic is checked only after it exits the per-node Envoy.
Two enforcement points: one before traffic arrives at the `ingress` identity, and one after, when it is about to exit the per-node Envoy.
Three enforcement points: at the external boundary, at the Envoy proxy, and at the backend service.
Two enforcement points: one for Ingress traffic and one for Gateway API traffic, which are handled separately.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt identifies exactly two logical enforcement points, not three.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states the same principles apply to Gateway API, but the two enforcement points are defined by the traffic's position relative to the ``ingress`` identity and the Envoy exit, not by the API type.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator notices that an external load balancer is failing to forward traffic correctly to a Service exposing Cilium's Envoy with `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` set. According to the excerpt, how does Cilium handle the `healthCheckNodePort` check in this scenario?

options.text: Cilium ensures that every node in the cluster will pass the `healthCheckNodePort` check.
Cilium disables the `healthCheckNodePort` check entirely for Envoy services.
Only nodes with local Envoy pods running will pass the check, causing the load balancer to drop traffic to other nodes.
The check returns a non-200 status on all nodes to force the load balancer to use a different policy.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that for any Services that expose Cilium's Envoy, Cilium will ensure that when `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` is set, every node in the cluster will pass the `healthCheckNodePort` check, so that external load balancers will forward correctly.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not disable the check; it ensures it passes on all nodes.
optionRationale.c: This is the default Kubernetes behaviour for `Local` policy, but Cilium modifies this behaviour for Envoy services to ensure all nodes pass.
